content:
Facts: A nephew of the deceased challenged a holographic will appointing another relative as sole heir, alleging forgery and lack of handwriting. Several alleged heirs intervened in support of the challenge. The defendant objected, inter alia, to the plaintiff’s lack of standing, arguing that his status as legitimate heir had not been duly proven.

Legal framework
Articles 565 ff. ICC on intestate succession and kinship; Article 2697 ICC on burden of proof; Articles 300, 307 and 125 CPC on interruption and resumption of proceedings; rules on civil evidence and administrative declarations (Presidential Decree No. 445/2000); settled Supreme Court case law on proof of heirship.

Interpretative issue
Whether the standing to challenge a will requires strict proof of the claimant’s status as legitimate heir, and whether declarations in lieu of affidavits or administrative documents may suffice as evidence in civil proceedings.

Principle applied
Standing to contest a will presupposes strict proof of the claimant’s status as heir, which must be established through civil status records demonstrating kinship with the deceased. Declarations in lieu of affidavits and succession declarations, while admissible for administrative purposes, have no evidentiary value in civil proceedings and cannot satisfy the burden of proof under Article 2697 ICC. In the absence of proper documentary proof of heirship, the action is inadmissible for lack of standing and must be dismissed, irrespective of the merits of the alleged testamentary invalidity.
